extracted.intended_audience: U.S. design patent applicants, inventors, small businesses considering foreign design protection
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for U.S. applicants on obtaining foreign design patent protection, including timing/priority rules, use of the Hague Agreement, country-specific requirements (e.g., drawings), costs, and whether to engage local counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid public disclosure before first filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Check to make sure you did not publicly disclose your design before filing your first design patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike the US, most foreign countries require that you secure a patent priority date before publicly disclosing your invention. Public disclosure prior to obtaining a priority date can destroy foreign rights. Confirm no public disclosures occurred before filing if you intend to seek foreign protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority/filing deadline for foreign design applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The deadline for filing a foreign design patent application that will get the benefit of your earlier US filing date is 6 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If over 6 months have passed since your US filing date, you might still be able to file foreign design applications without the priority claim as long as you have not made any public disclosures. Be mindful of this 6‑month window to preserve priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether foreign protection is needed based on knockoff risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain foreign patents if competitors are likely to make knockoff products in foreign countries; foreign protection can enable you to stop foreign manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your products are simpler and easier to copy, consider filing counterpart design applications in countries (for example, China) where knockoffs are likely. Weigh the cost of foreign filings against the commercial risk of foreign copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget for country-dependent filing and prosecution costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial filing costs vary depending upon each foreign country; example given: China initial filing cost may range from $1,500 to $2,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind additional costs for ongoing prosecution, including issue fees if and when your design patent application is allowed. Plan for both filing and post-filing prosecution expenses when deciding where to file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider using the Hague Agreement for multi-country protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Hague Agreement (U.S. participant since May 13, 2015), U.S. applicants can file a single design patent application and seek protection in multiple member countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hague streamlines filing in multiple member countries so applicants no longer need to file individual design patent applications in each desired member country. Consider Hague when seeking protection across several member countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand term and publication effects of Hague and U.S. filings
rubrics_metrics.description: For U.S. design patent applications filed on or after May 13, 2015, the term was extended from 14 to 15 years from the issue date even if the Hague process is not used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International design patent applications under the Hague system will generally be published 6 months after the filing date, which can provide potential provisional rights that predate the grant date, but those provisional rights apply only for a single embodiment. Factor term length and publication consequences into strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use local IP firms for country-specific filing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Each country has its own rules regarding design patent drawings; the firm prefers to have individual design patent applications filed in foreign countries using local IP firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working with local patent experts can save time and money by addressing potential issues upfront. Local counsel expertise is effective for complying with country-specific formalities (e.g., drawing standards) and for handling prosecution in-country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on local experts to save time and money
rubrics_metrics.description: Working with local patent experts can save time and money in the long run by dealing with potential issues upfront.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage local attorneys to handle nuances of foreign prosecution and to potentially avoid costly corrections or re-filings. Using local counsel is presented as a practical best practice rather than an optional extra.
